metadata.title: CP-Dysarthria Domain Glossary
metadata.authors: Victor & Shintaro (L665, Fall 2026); drafted with Claude Code, to be reviewed by the team
metadata.domain: Cerebral palsy (CP)-associated dysarthria, related motor speech disorders, their clinical assessment and treatment, and dysarthric speech technology.
metadata.format: Compatible with the course build_ner_corpus.py loader (entries[].concept_label/term/acronym). Extra fields: id (stable concept identifier), hypernym, mesh_id, acronym_requires_long_form, notes.

labels.DISORDER: A disease, disorder, or clinical motor sign: dysarthria and its subtypes, cerebral palsy and its subtypes, other neurological conditions that cause dysarthria (Parkinson's disease, ALS, stroke, ...), and related speech, language, and swallowing disorders.
labels.SPEECH_FEATURE: A perceptual or acoustic property of speech that is affected in dysarthria or used to describe it, such as intelligibility, hypernasality, speech rate, or jitter. Not the disorder itself and not the test used to measure it.
labels.ASSESSMENT: A named clinical instrument, rating scale, or classification system used to evaluate speech, communication, or motor function, such as the Frenchay Dysarthria Assessment or GMFCS.
labels.TREATMENT: A clinical intervention, therapy, device, or drug used to manage dysarthria, communication impairment, or the underlying motor disorder.
labels.SPEECH_TECH: A speech-technology task, model, acoustic representation, or evaluation metric used to process, recognize, synthesize, or analyse (dysarthric) speech, such as ASR, wav2vec 2.0, MFCC, or WER.
labels.DATASET: A named speech corpus or database used in dysarthric speech research, such as UASpeech or TORGO.

metadata.acronym_policy: Acronyms are matched case-sensitively. Acronyms with acronym_requires_long_form=true are only labelled in documents that also contain one of the concept's terms, because they have frequent unrelated readings in the corpus (e.g. FDA = US Food and Drug Administration, SGD = stochastic gradient descent).
metadata.review_status: Draft: definitions are paraphrased from the cited sources; every source URL was checked to resolve on 2026-10-29 (see glossary_verification.json). Team review pending.
metadata.removed_concepts: TRT008 selective dorsal rhizotomy and TRT012 nonspeech oral motor exercises were drafted but removed on 2026-10-29 because they never occur in the corpus (the corpus uses 'oral motor' only for tasks/examinations).

definition: A motor speech disorder in which weakness, slowness, or poor coordination of the speech muscles, caused by damage to the central or peripheral nervous system, impairs respiration, phonation, resonance, articulation, and/or prosody, while language itself is intact.

Dysarthria caused by bilateral upper motor neuron damage, typically with strained-strangled voice, slow rate, hypernasality, and imprecise consonants; the dysarthria type most often associated with spastic cerebral palsy.
Dysarthria caused by lower motor neuron damage (cranial or spinal nerves), characterized by weakness, breathiness, hypernasality, and nasal emission.
Dysarthria caused by cerebellar damage, with irregular articulatory breakdowns, excess and equal stress, and poorly coordinated, scanning speech.
Dysarthria associated with basal ganglia control-circuit damage, typically in Parkinson's disease, with reduced loudness, monopitch, short rushes of speech, and imprecise consonants.
Dysarthria caused by involuntary movements from basal ganglia disorders (e.g., chorea, dystonia), producing variable rate, loudness, and articulation.
Dysarthria combining features of two or more single dysarthria types, as in ALS (spastic-flaccid) or multiple sclerosis (ataxic-spastic).

A group of permanent, non-progressive disorders of movement and posture caused by injury to or abnormal development of the immature brain before, during, or shortly after birth; speech is frequently affected by dysarthria.
entries.notes: CP is unambiguous in this corpus (spot-checked 2026-10-29).

definition: The most common subtype of cerebral palsy, marked by increased muscle tone (spasticity); classified by the limbs involved (diplegia, hemiplegia, quadriplegia).
A subtype of cerebral palsy with involuntary, uncontrolled movements (athetosis, chorea, dystonia) caused mainly by basal ganglia injury.
A progressive neurodegenerative disease caused by loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, with tremor, rigidity, slowness of movement, and often hypokinetic dysarthria.
A progressive, usually fatal degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons causing weakness, atrophy, dysphagia, and mixed spastic-flaccid dysarthria.
An autoimmune disease in which demyelination of the central nervous system causes variable neurological symptoms, including ataxic and spastic dysarthria.
entries.notes: MS also occurs as author initials and abbreviations in the corpus.

definition: Sudden loss of neurological function caused by interrupted blood supply (ischemia) or bleeding in the brain; a frequent cause of acquired dysarthria and aphasia in adults.
entries.notes: Also matches 'stroke' in non-medical senses (e.g. pen stroke); rare in this corpus.

definition: Brain damage caused by an external mechanical force, such as a blow to the head; a cause of acquired dysarthria.
A motor speech disorder in which the planning or programming of speech movements is impaired, without weakness of the speech muscles.
A pediatric motor speech disorder affecting the precision and consistency of speech movements because of impaired motor planning, in the absence of neuromuscular deficits.
A speech disorder caused by impaired planning, programming, control, or execution of speech movements; the two main types are dysarthria and apraxia of speech.

An acquired language disorder, usually after left-hemisphere damage, impairing the comprehension and/or production of spoken or written language; distinct from dysarthria, which affects speech motor control.
Difficulty swallowing, often co-occurring with dysarthria because both involve the oral and pharyngeal musculature.
Impaired voice production, with abnormal pitch, loudness, or voice quality, resulting from structural, neurological, or functional causes.
A chromosomal disorder caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21, associated with hypotonia, intellectual disability, and frequent speech and motor speech disorders.
An inherited neurodegenerative disease causing chorea, cognitive decline, and hyperkinetic dysarthria.
Velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone caused by upper motor neuron damage; the defining motor sign of spastic cerebral palsy and spastic dysarthria.
A movement disorder with sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contractions causing abnormal postures or twisting movements; common in dyskinetic cerebral palsy.
Impaired coordination of voluntary movement, usually from cerebellar damage; in speech it produces ataxic dysarthria.
A group of diseases in which upper and/or lower motor neurons degenerate, including ALS; often causes spastic and/or flaccid dysarthria.
A subtype of cerebral palsy caused mainly by cerebellar injury, with impaired balance and coordination; speech may show ataxic features.
The degree to which a speaker's intended message is understood by a listener; the primary functional outcome measure in dysarthria.
Excessive nasal resonance on oral speech sounds because the velopharyngeal port does not close adequately; common in spastic and flaccid dysarthria.
Consonants produced with reduced accuracy or distorted place or manner of articulation; one of the most frequent perceptual features across dysarthria types.
How fast a person speaks, usually measured in syllables or words per unit time (articulation rate excludes pauses); typically reduced in spastic dysarthria.
The rhythm, stress, and intonation patterns of speech, carried by variations in pitch, loudness, and duration; often reduced or disrupted in dysarthria.
Reduced pitch variation, making speech sound flat; a characteristic of hypokinetic and spastic dysarthria.
Reduced variation in loudness across an utterance.
A voice quality with audible air escape caused by incomplete vocal fold closure; typical of flaccid dysarthria.
A rough, effortful voice quality caused by excessive laryngeal tension; strained-strangled voice is a hallmark of spastic dysarthria.
The characteristic sound of a speaker's voice apart from pitch and loudness, shaped by phonation and resonance (e.g., breathy, harsh, hoarse).
The rate of vocal fold vibration, the main acoustic correlate of perceived pitch; its mean and variability are standard acoustic measures in dysarthria.
A resonance peak of the vocal tract (F1, F2, ...) that determines vowel quality; formant patterns reflect tongue and jaw movement.
The area of the polygon formed by the first two formant frequencies of the corner vowels; a smaller vowel space indicates reduced articulatory range and lower intelligibility.
Cycle-to-cycle variation in the period of vocal fold vibration (frequency perturbation); a measure of voice instability.
entries.notes: Rarely used in its everyday sense in this corpus.

definition: Cycle-to-cycle variation in the amplitude of vocal fold vibration (amplitude perturbation).
The ratio of periodic (harmonic) to aperiodic (noise) energy in the voice signal; lower values indicate a breathier or hoarser voice.
The speed and regularity of rapidly repeated syllables such as /pa/, /ta/, /ka/ or /pataka/; used to assess oral motor speech control.
The longest time a person can sustain a vowel on one breath; reflects respiratory and laryngeal efficiency.
The production of speech sounds by movements of the lips, tongue, jaw, and velum; one of the speech subsystems affected in dysarthria.
entries.notes: Also used in non-speech senses (e.g. articulation of a theory); rare in this corpus.

definition: The production of voice by vibration of the vocal folds driven by exhaled air; one of the speech subsystems affected in dysarthria.
The interval between the release of a stop consonant and the onset of vocal fold vibration; distinguishes voiced from voiceless stops and is often disrupted in dysarthria.
How normal or typical speech sounds to listeners, independent of intelligibility; often reduced by prosodic abnormalities in dysarthria.
A standardized clinical test that rates reflexes, respiration, lips, palate, laryngeal function, tongue, and intelligibility to describe the severity and type of dysarthria.
entries.notes: FDA also denotes the US Food and Drug Administration in some documents; hence the long-form requirement.

definition: A five-level system that classifies the self-initiated gross motor function (sitting, walking, mobility) of children and young people with cerebral palsy.
A five-level system that classifies how children with cerebral palsy use their hands to handle objects in daily activities.
entries.notes: The corpus also uses the variant name 'Manual Ability Classification Scale'.

definition: A five-level system that classifies the everyday communication performance of people with cerebral palsy as senders and receivers of messages.
A four-level scale that classifies the speech production of children with cerebral palsy, from no apparent speech impairment to no understandable speech.

term: Assessment of Intelligibility of Dysarthric Speech
Computerized Assessment of Intelligibility of Dysarthric Speech
definition: A standardized test in which listeners transcribe a speaker's single words and sentences to quantify intelligibility and speaking rate in dysarthria (Yorkston & Beukelman).
entries.notes: Provenance is a corpus document (systematic review of dysarthria outcome measures) that describes the instrument; the original 1981 manual is not online. AIDS requires the long form (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome).

term: MDS Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale
definition: A clinical rating scale for the severity of Parkinson's disease covering non-motor and motor experiences of daily living, a motor examination (including speech), and motor complications.
A 12-item questionnaire rating bulbar (including speech), fine motor, gross motor, and respiratory function in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
Clinical judgement of speech characteristics by trained listeners, the reference standard for describing dysarthria type and severity.
Standard perceptual voice rating protocols: CAPE-V rates overall severity, roughness, breathiness, strain, pitch, and loudness; GRBAS rates grade, roughness, breathiness, asthenia, and strain.
Treatment by a speech-language pathologist to improve speech, language, or communication, e.g. exercises for respiration, phonation, articulation, and prosody, and compensatory strategies.
entries.notes: SLT also names the IEEE Spoken Language Technology workshop.

definition: Methods and tools (signs, picture boards, speech-generating devices) that supplement or replace natural speech for people with severe communication impairment.
An electronic AAC device that produces synthesized or recorded speech output for the user.
entries.notes: SGD also means stochastic gradient descent in the ML papers; hence the long-form requirement.

definition: An intensive, standardized voice treatment that trains increased vocal loudness, developed for hypokinetic dysarthria in Parkinson's disease and also applied in cerebral palsy.
A neurotoxin injected into overactive muscles to reduce spasticity or dystonia, used in cerebral palsy and in some voice disorders.
A GABA-B receptor agonist muscle relaxant, given orally or intrathecally, used to reduce spasticity.
Surgical implantation of electrodes that deliver electrical stimulation to deep brain structures to treat movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease and dystonia.
Rehabilitation using exercise and physical methods to improve movement, strength, posture, and mobility.
Rehabilitation that helps people perform everyday activities, including fine motor and self-care skills.
A technique that gives a person real-time information about a physiological signal (e.g., loudness, pitch, or articulator movement) so they can learn to control it.
Technology that automatically converts spoken audio into text; standard systems perform poorly on dysarthric speech, motivating adaptation research.
entries.notes: ASR is unambiguous here, but DSR could mean distant speech recognition, so acronyms require a long form in the document; ASR is defined in practically every ASR paper.

definition: The standard ASR evaluation metric: the number of word substitutions, deletions, and insertions divided by the number of words in the reference transcript.
Error rates computed like WER but over characters or phonemes instead of words; used for languages without word spacing and for sub-word evaluation.
A compact spectral representation of speech computed from the cepstrum of a mel-scaled filterbank; a standard input feature for speech recognition and dysarthria classification.
A time-frequency representation of audio whose frequency axis is warped to the mel scale (often log-compressed); the standard input to neural speech models.
A self-supervised speech representation model that learns from raw audio by contrastive prediction of masked latent units, then is fine-tuned for ASR or classification.
Hidden-Unit BERT: a self-supervised speech model trained to predict masked cluster labels of the audio.
A self-supervised speech model trained with masked speech prediction and denoising for full-stack speech processing tasks.
OpenAI's encoder-decoder speech recognition model trained with large-scale weak supervision on multilingual web audio.
entries.notes: Lower-case 'whisper' in this corpus almost always also refers to the model (e.g. whisper-small).

definition: A convolution-augmented Transformer architecture for speech recognition that models both local and global dependencies.
A training objective and decoding method that lets neural networks map unsegmented audio to label sequences without frame-level alignment.
A statistical sequence model with hidden states; the basis of classical ASR systems (GMM-HMM, hybrid DNN-HMM).
Transforming speech so that it sounds like another speaker or speaking style while keeping the content; used to convert dysarthric to typical speech or to generate training data.
entries.notes: Provenance: corpus papers on dysarthric voice conversion. VC requires the long form because it is a short, generic abbreviation.

definition: Technology that generates spoken audio from text; used in AAC devices and for synthesizing dysarthric training data.
Adjusting a speech recognition model to an individual speaker's voice with a small amount of their data, a key strategy for dysarthric ASR.
Data augmentation that resamples or time-stretches training audio to create faster or slower copies; tempo perturbation is used to simulate slow dysarthric speech.
Learning representations from unlabeled data by solving pretext tasks (e.g., predicting masked audio); the training paradigm of wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, and WavLM.
Automatically aligning a known transcript to audio to obtain word or phone boundaries.
entries.notes: Provenance is a corpus document on forced alignment for speech-language pathology.

definition: Fixed-length speaker embeddings extracted from a deep neural network, used for speaker recognition and as features for dysarthria detection.
Low-dimensional speaker and channel representations from total variability factor analysis, used for speaker verification and adaptation.
A phone-level score, derived from ASR posteriors, of how closely a pronunciation matches the canonical one; used to assess atypical speech.
The average of listener ratings (usually on a 1-5 scale) of speech quality or naturalness, used to evaluate synthesized or converted speech.
Automatic classification of speech recordings as dysarthric vs. typical, or into severity levels, from acoustic features or learned representations.
entries.notes: Provenance are corpus documents describing the task.

definition: A dysarthric speech database recorded at the University of Illinois with isolated-word audio from speakers with dysarthria, most of them with cerebral palsy, and control speakers.
A database of acoustic and articulatory (EMA) speech from speakers with dysarthria due to cerebral palsy or ALS and matched controls, recorded at the University of Toronto.
An early database of nonsense sentences read by male speakers with dysarthria, with phonetic transcriptions.
An Italian dysarthric speech corpus of voice commands from speakers with dysarthria and healthy controls.
A large, community-supported collection of speech from people with Parkinson's disease, ALS, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, and stroke, created to improve ASR accessibility.
A 1000-hour corpus of read English audiobook speech from typical speakers, widely used to pre-train or benchmark ASR.
A Colombian Spanish speech corpus of people with Parkinson's disease and matched healthy controls.
A Mandarin Chinese speech database of speakers with dysarthria, used for dysarthric ASR research.
A crowd-sourced, multilingual corpus of read speech released by Mozilla.
An audio-visual database of British English emotional speech from speakers with dysarthria and typical speakers.
